title: Bananas (per lb)

drivers.name: New competitor across the street
drivers.evidence: One past occurrence of competitor entry near this store; noise-adjusted estimate suggests ~7% demand drop, but evidence is thin. No promotion to offset.

drivers.name: Price increase to $0.68 (+1.5%)
drivers.evidence: No past lift observed at $0.68; price increase likely reduces demand. Combined with competitor, effect is modest but negative.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median of 438.2 is stable, with no seasonal ramp or trend change. The target week has no event, but a 1.5% price increase to $0.68 and a new competitor across the street. Price increases typically reduce demand; historical data shows no lift at $0.68. Competitor entry likely hurts sales, especially with no promotion to offset. The classical uplift model suggests +37% from Thanksgiving, but that is irrelevant here—no holiday. The noise-adjusted effect of a competitor entry is uncertain (one past occurrence), and the price rise may lower demand by ~5–8%. We shrink the effect toward 1.0 due to thin evidence and high noise. No drivers justify a multiplier >1.0.

TARGET WEEK: 2026-11-16 to 2026-11-22 (6 weeks after the last week with sales data)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 0.68 (+1.5% vs regular price 0.67)
  planner notes: A competitor opens a store across the street this week

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 438.2 | 5%-95%: 312.4 - 556.2 | 10%-90%: 346.4 - 529.2

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-21% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
